lessons.title: Exact square roots and square factors
lessons.summary: Recognise a surd, locate it between integers and extract the largest square factor.
lessons.objective: Recognise a surd, locate it between integers and extract the largest square factor.
lessons.before: Recall the first ten perfect squares. Use the positive square root when finding a length.
lessons.ideas:
A surd is an exact irrational root. In \(3<\sqrt{14}<4\), the middle term gives the value exactly and the outer numbers show its size. A finite calculator display such as \(3.742\) gives an approximation.

Use \(\sqrt{k^2d}=k\sqrt d\) for positive integer \(k\). Choose the largest square factor you can find. You may take out smaller factors one at a time, provided you stop only when none remain.

If the question gives an outside multiplier already, multiply it by the factor taken out. Leave a square-free radicand in the result.
lessons.method:
When is a square root an exact surd?

When the positive integer inside a square root is a perfect square, its root is an integer. If that integer is between two consecutive squares, its square root lies between the corresponding two integers.

How do I take a square factor out?

Start with a square that divides the radicand exactly. Divisibility matters because the leftover factor must still be an integer.

How do I use the same idea for a length?

A square with area given has an exact side length equal to the positive square root of that area. Multiplying a length by a scale factor multiplies the entire expression.
mistakes: The square root sign denotes the non-negative root. The equation \(x^2=14\) has two solutions, whereas \(\sqrt{14}\) is a single positive number.
For \(\sqrt{63}\), use \(63=9\times 7\). The square root of 9 is 3, so the multiplier outside the root is 3.
If you double a side length, its square area is multiplied by four. Doubling a number under a root does not double the root.

examples.title: Distinguish exact square roots
examples.question:
One of \(\sqrt{9}\) and \(\sqrt{10}\) is an integer and one is not. Which set contains \(\sqrt{10}\)?

  1. Integers
  2. Irrational numbers
  3. Non-integer rational numbers
examples.solution:
The neighbouring squares are \(9\) and \(16\).

\(10\) lies strictly between them and is an integer that is not a perfect square.

The square root of a non-square positive integer is irrational. The comparison \(3<\sqrt{10}<4\) locates its value.

examples.title: Take out a square factor
examples.question: Write \(\sqrt{45}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{5}\). Find \(a\).
examples.solution:
Look for a perfect square that divides \(45\).

\(45=9\times 5\), so \(\sqrt{45}=\sqrt{9}\times \sqrt{5}\). The first root is \(3\).

The fully simplified result is \(3\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=3\).

examples.title: Multiply the outside coefficients
examples.question: Write \(2\sqrt{63}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\).
examples.solution:
Factor the radicand as \(9\times 7\).

Use \(\sqrt{63}=3\sqrt{7}\). The two coefficients multiply to \(2\times 3=6\).

The fully simplified result is \(6\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=6\).

lessons.title: Add, subtract, multiply and divide surds
lessons.summary: Decide when to collect matching radicals and when to combine two radicands.
lessons.objective: Decide when to collect matching radicals and when to combine two radicands.
lessons.before: Be able to simplify a square root before comparing its radicand with another one.
lessons.ideas:
Think of \(\sqrt5\) as the common factor in \(4\sqrt5+3\sqrt5\). Adding the coefficients gives \(7\sqrt5\). If one root is still unsimplified, simplify it first.

For non-negative radicands \(a,b\), use \(\sqrt a\sqrt b=\sqrt{ab}\). Any coefficients outside the roots also multiply. Simplify the resulting root if it has a square factor.

For \(a\geq0,\ b>0\), \(\frac{\sqrt a}{\sqrt b}=\sqrt{\frac ab}\). The square of \(k\sqrt d\) is \(k^2d\).
lessons.method:
When can I collect two surds?

Identify what the operation does before moving anything under or out of the root. A sum or difference can be collected when the simplified radical parts match.

What changes if the operation is multiplication?

The simplification test comes first. If the square-free radicands differ, the sum stays as separate terms. A product follows a different rule.

How do I divide or square exact roots?

The quotient can be put under a single radical with a strictly positive denominator. Squaring a single surd term multiplies it by itself.
mistakes: Subtract the outside coefficient and preserve the radicand. Never subtract the radicands because the two terms are joined by subtraction.
The radical multiplication rule cannot be used for addition. For example, \(\sqrt2+\sqrt3\ne\sqrt5\).
Squaring a product squares both factors. A square with side \(4\sqrt3\) has area \(16\times3=48\), not 12.

examples.title: Collect like surds
examples.question: Write \(\sqrt{150}+\sqrt{24}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{6}\). Find \(a\).
examples.solution:
Simplify each term first. \(\sqrt{150}=5\sqrt{6}\) and \(\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt{6}\).

The radicals now match. Use the coefficient calculation \(5+2=7\) and keep the radical.

The fully simplified result is \(7\sqrt{6}\), so \(a=7\).

examples.title: Recognise unlike radicals
examples.question:
Choose the fully simplified form of \(\sqrt{12}+\sqrt{63}\).

  1. \(2\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{7}\)
  2. \(\sqrt{75}\)
  3. \(5\sqrt{3}\)
  4. \(2\sqrt{7}+3\sqrt{3}\)
examples.solution:
The first square factor is \(4\) and the second is \(9\).

The simplified terms are \(2\sqrt{3}\) and \(3\sqrt{7}\).

The square-free radicands differ, so leave the exact sum as \(2\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{7}\).

examples.title: Divide two square roots
examples.question: Write \(\frac{\sqrt{84}}{\sqrt{3}}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{7}\). Find \(a\).
examples.solution:
The denominator is positive. Divide inside one radical to give \(\sqrt{28}\).

The simplified radicand still has square factor \(4\). Extract it to find the coefficient.

The fully simplified result is \(2\sqrt{7}\), so \(a=2\).

lessons.title: Expand brackets with surds
lessons.summary: Write every product in a bracket expansion, then collect rational and irrational terms.
lessons.objective: Write every product in a bracket expansion, then collect rational and irrational terms.
lessons.before: Remember that a product of two copies of the same square root is the radicand.
lessons.ideas:
The product of one surd and an integer usually stays as a surd. A pair of matching square roots multiplies to an integer. Write these contributions as separate terms.

Set out four products in a line or grid. First collect the rational products, then collect the signed coefficients of the matching radicals.

Use \((u+v)(u-v)=u^2-v^2\) only after checking for those opposite signs. For a rectangular area, use the full length times the full width.
lessons.method:
How do I distribute a surd across a bracket?

The same distributive rule works for rational numbers and surds. Start by showing explicitly which two terms the outside factor multiplies.

How do I keep track of all four products?

Each term of the first bracket multiplies each term of the second. For a square, both brackets are identical, so the middle terms match rather than cancel.

When do the cross terms cancel?

When the brackets have the same terms with opposite signs between them, one cross product is the negative of the other.
mistakes: Stopping after multiplying the first term leaves out part of the bracket. Count how many terms were inside it.
Squaring a difference still gives a positive square of the second term. The middle terms of an expansion like \((a-b)^2\) are both negative.
The result of multiplying opposite-sign brackets can be negative. Check the order of the two squares instead of taking their absolute difference.

examples.title: Expand one surd across a bracket
examples.question: Write \(2\sqrt{5}\left(3+\sqrt{5}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{5}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
examples.solution:
Multiply the outside surd by both terms inside the bracket.

The two products are \(6\sqrt{5}\) and \(2\times 5\). The second product is rational because the two roots match.

The resulting expression is \(10+6\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=10\) and \(b=6\).

examples.title: Track negative terms in an expansion
examples.question: Write \(\left(2-2\sqrt{6}\right)\left(4+\sqrt{6}\right)\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{6}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
examples.solution:
The product of the two rational terms is \(8\). The product of the two surd terms is \(-12\).

The middle terms are \(2\sqrt{6}\) and \(-8\sqrt{6}\). Combine their signed coefficients.

The resulting expression is \(-4-6\sqrt{6}\), so \(a=-4\) and \(b=-6\).

examples.title: Spot a difference of two squares
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(\left(7+2\sqrt{5}\right)\left(7-2\sqrt{5}\right)\).
examples.solution:
The two brackets have matching rational parts. Their radical terms have opposite signs.

The cross terms cancel. The rational result is \(7^2-2^2\times 5=29\).

lessons.title: Rationalise a one-term denominator
lessons.summary: Use a factor equal to one to clear a radical from a denominator and reduce the fraction.
lessons.objective: Use a factor equal to one to clear a radical from a denominator and reduce the fraction.
lessons.before: Know how to simplify a root and reduce a numerical fraction by a common factor.
lessons.ideas:
If the denominator is \(\sqrt d\), multiply both parts of the fraction by \(\sqrt d\). The common multiplier is nonzero. The denominator now contains \(\sqrt d\times\sqrt d=d\).

In \(\frac{3}{2\sqrt7}\), multiplying by \(\frac{\sqrt7}{\sqrt7}\) produces a denominator of \(14\). In a root of a fraction, splitting the roots can reveal an ordinary surd denominator.

For \(\frac{6\sqrt5}{8\sqrt5}\), first cancel \(\sqrt5\), then reduce \(\frac68\) to \(\frac34\).
lessons.method:
How do I change the form without changing the value?

Rationalising a denominator means rewriting the same value with a rational number at the bottom. The numerator may still contain a surd.

How do I handle a coefficient or a square factor?

When the denominator is a multiple of a root, only the radical factor needs another copy of itself. Simplify a radicand with square factors before choosing the multiplier.

When can I cancel instead of multiplying?

Check whether the same root is already a factor of the entire numerator and the entire denominator. If it is, cancelling that nonzero common factor makes the denominator rational.
mistakes: Multiplying only the bottom changes the value. The whole fraction must be multiplied by a fraction equal to one.
The root in the denominator may simplify first. Rationalising a larger expression immediately can leave an unnecessarily complicated fraction.
Cancellation only removes common factors. The term \(\sqrt5\) cannot be cancelled from the sum \(6+\sqrt5\).

examples.title: Rationalise a single square root
examples.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{7}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{7}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
examples.solution:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{7}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.

The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{7}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{3}{7}=\frac{3}{7}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{7}\).

examples.title: Rationalise a multiple of a square root
examples.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{3}{2\sqrt{6}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{6}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
examples.solution:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{6}\). The fraction made from two copies of that root is 1.

The unreduced rationalised result is \(\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{12}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{3}{12}=\frac{1}{4}\). The simplified expression is \(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\).

examples.title: Simplify a radical before rationalising
examples.question: Write \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{27}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{3}}{b}\) with coprime positive integers \(a\) and \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).
examples.solution:
Take the square factor out of the denominator to give \(\frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}\).

Multiply both the numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{3}\). This gives \(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}\).

Reduce the numerical fraction \(\frac{2}{9}=\frac{2}{9}\) to obtain \(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}\).

lessons.title: Rationalise with conjugates
lessons.summary: Use the matching sign change to eliminate a surd from a two-term denominator and solve mixed problems.
lessons.objective: Use the matching sign change to eliminate a surd from a two-term denominator and solve mixed problems.
lessons.before: Be able to rationalise one radical and use a difference of two squares.
lessons.ideas:
For \(a+b\sqrt d\), use \(a-b\sqrt d\). The cross terms cancel, and the denominator becomes \(a^2-b^2d\). Multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate preserves the exact value.

If the denominator is negative, move the negative sign through the entire numerator. Divide all integer coefficients and the denominator by their common factor before reading the requested values.

When two different fractions have conjugate denominators, there is a convenient common rational denominator. Work with each numerator as a whole before adding or subtracting.
lessons.method:
Which multiplier clears a two-term denominator?

A denominator with two terms needs a whole bracket as its multiplier. Find the bracket with the same two pieces but the opposite sign on the radical term.

How do I reduce a rationalised result?

After rationalising, expand the numerator if the question asks for a coefficient form. The result at the bottom is a nonzero rational number.

How do I choose a route in a mixed problem?

Look at each term separately. A root with a square factor can be simplified first. A fraction with a radical denominator can be rationalised first. Combine matching radicals after those steps.
mistakes: Multiplying by the root alone usually leaves a radical from the rational term. It cannot clear both terms.
In \(\frac{4-2\sqrt3}{-6}\), changing the denominator to 6 also changes both signs in the numerator. Cancelling requires a factor shared by both numerator terms and the denominator.
A minus between fractions subtracts the second numerator in full. It changes every term in that numerator.

examples.title: Choose a rationalising multiplier
examples.question:
Which multiplier makes \(4+2\sqrt{7}\) rational when used in a product?

  1. \(4-2\sqrt{7}\)
  2. \(2\sqrt{7}\)
  3. \(4+2\sqrt{7}\)
  4. \(4\)
examples.solution:
The product must have no surviving radical component. Use the bracket with the same rational part and the opposite radical part.

Multiplying by \(4-2\sqrt{7}\) gives \(4^2-4\times 7=-12\).

examples.title: Use a conjugate when the radical already has a coefficient
examples.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\frac{52}{8+2\sqrt{3}}\). Give the two integers \(a\) and \(b\) in the form \(a+b\sqrt{3}\).
examples.solution:
Use \(8-2\sqrt{3}\) as the common multiplier. Its radical term has the opposite sign.

The bottom becomes \(8^2-4\times 3=52\) after the cross terms cancel.

The top becomes \(416-104\sqrt{3}\). Simplify the signs and common factors to obtain \(8-2\sqrt{3}\).

examples.title: Combine a simplified root and a rationalised fraction
examples.question: Write \(\sqrt{99}+\frac{22}{\sqrt{11}}\) in the form \(a\sqrt{11}\). Find \(a\).
examples.solution:
The first term is \(3\sqrt{11}\) after extracting the square factor.

Multiply top and bottom of the fraction by \(\sqrt{11}\). It simplifies to \(2\sqrt{11}\). Add the coefficients.

The fully simplified result is \(5\sqrt{11}\), so \(a=5\).

questions.title: Classify and bound a square root
questions.prompt_html:
1. One of \(\sqrt{100}\) and \(\sqrt{102}\) is an integer and one is not. Which set contains \(\sqrt{102}\)?

    1. Integers
    2. Irrational numbers
    3. Non-integer rational numbers

    Give a reason or show your working.

    [2]

  2. Find the consecutive integers \(a\) and \(b\) for which \(a<\sqrt{152}

    Write the complete exact result as well as the requested coefficient values. Show your working.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The neighbouring squares are \(100\) and \(121\).

\(102\) lies strictly between them and is an integer that is not a perfect square.

The square root of a non-square positive integer is irrational. The comparison \(10<\sqrt{102}<11\) locates its value.

(b)

Look for square numbers on both sides of \(152\).

\(12^2=144<152<169=13^2\).

Taking the positive square root of each number preserves this order, so the integers are \(12\) and \(13\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Check whether the integer under this square root is a perfect square.

(b) Find the largest square smaller than the number under the root.

marking_criteria.description_html: Compare the radicand with its neighbouring integer squares.
Give the complete exact result. Irrational numbers. \(10<\sqrt{102}<11\) Any algebraically valid method earns the same credit.
Find a pair of adjacent perfect squares on either side of the radicand.
Give the complete exact result. \(12<\sqrt{152}<13\) Any algebraically valid method earns the same credit.
